Why Open-Ended is Harder Than MCQ

In Matter open-ended questions, examiners are strict about the exact terminology you use. Saying "the air gets bigger" earns zero marks; you must specify that air gains heat and expands or that it occupies space. You also need to precisely identify the subject—whether it is the container or the substance inside.

Common P4 Open-Ended Writing Mistakes

These are the exact wording traps that cost students marks in the "Matter" topic.

Mistake 1: "Air is empty space"

What Students Write
"The bottle is empty so water goes in."
occupies space
0/1 marks
What to Write Instead
"Air occupies space in the bottle."
air
1/1 marks
The Fix: Never write that a seemingly empty container is "empty". Always state that air occupies space inside it.

Mistake 2: Squeezing Liquids

What Students Write
"The plunger pushed in because the water got squeezed."
compressed
0/2 marks
What to Write Instead
"Air can be compressed while water cannot."
compressed
2/2 marks
The Fix: Liquids have a definite volume. Only gases (like air) can be compressed.

Mistake 3: Disappearing Air in Sponges

What Students Write
"The sponge shrank to fit the container."
air escaped
0/2 marks
What to Write Instead
"The air inside the tiny spaces was squeezed out."
air
2/2 marks
The Fix: Solids do not change volume spontaneously. If a sponge compresses, explain that the air pockets inside it were squeezed out.

Mistake 4: Solid Object Heating

What Students Write
"The plastic ping pong ball expanded in hot water."
air gains heat
0/2 marks
What to Write Instead
"Air in the ping pong ball gains heat and expands."
expands
2/2 marks
The Fix: Always identify what is actually expanding. In balloons and ping pong balls, it is the internal air, not the external shell.

Mistake 5: Shadows as Matter

What Students Write
"A shadow is matter because I can see it."
occupies space
0/1 marks
What to Write Instead
"A shadow is not a matter as it does not occupy space."
matter
1/1 marks
The Fix: The definition of matter depends on mass and volume (space), not visibility.

Mistake 6: Holes and Air Flow

What Students Write
"Water entered Cup B because it has a hole."
air escaped
0/2 marks
What to Write Instead
"The hole allowed the air to escape so water could enter."
escape
2/2 marks
The Fix: Always describe the flow of air. Water cannot enter a space until the existing air vacates it.

Mistake 7: Pouring Liquids Changes Volume

What Students Write
"The volume of water increased because the new container is wider."
definite volume
0/1 marks
What to Write Instead
"Water has a definite volume."
definite volume
1/1 marks
The Fix: Liquid volume is constant. Changing the container changes the shape, not the amount of space it takes up.

Mistake 8: Mass equals Volume

What Students Write
"The metal ball is heavier so it will cause the water level to rise more."
same volume
0/1 marks
What to Write Instead
"The metal ball has the same volume as the plastic ball."
volume
1/1 marks
The Fix: Water displacement measures volume, not mass. Objects of the same size displace the same amount of water, regardless of weight.

Critical Distinctions for P4

Air vs Water Compressibility

Air
  • Gas state
  • Has no definite volume
  • Can be compressed
Water
  • Liquid state
  • Has a definite volume
  • Cannot be compressed
How to Write the Compare Answer:
"Air can be compressed while water cannot be compressed."
Why Students Confuse These: Both flow and take the shape of their container, but only gases can change their total volume.

Definite Shape vs Takes Shape of Container

Solid
  • Has a definite shape
  • Cannot flow
  • Remains the same shape when moved
Liquid / Gas
  • Has no definite shape
  • Takes the shape of its container
  • Can flow easily
How to Write the Compare Answer:
"A solid has a definite shape but a liquid has no definite shape."
Why Students Confuse These: They think powders or sand are liquids because they pour, but each grain is a tiny solid with a definite shape.

Mass vs Volume

Mass
  • Amount of matter
  • Makes things heavy
  • Does not depend on size
Volume
  • Amount of space occupied
  • Dictates size/displacement
  • Unrelated to heaviness
How to Write the Compare Answer:
"Two objects of the same volume can have different masses."
Why Students Confuse These: A common misconception is that a heavier object always takes up more space.

Waterproof vs Flexible

Waterproof
  • Material does not absorb water
  • Suitable for raincoats/umbrellas
Flexible
  • Material can be stretched or bent
  • Opposite of rigid
How to Write the Compare Answer:
"Material A is waterproof, but material C is not waterproof."
Why Students Confuse These: They confuse the purpose of a material property when evaluating tables.

Linking Words

Use these to structure your answers: while, instead of, as, since. They help contrast properties (e.g., "Air can be compressed while water cannot").

Wrong Written Answers — P4 Traps

Trap 1: Shadows are matter.

Students assume shadows are matter because they can be seen and appear to take up physical shape on the ground.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

A shadow is not matter because it has no mass and does not occupy space.

Use strict definitions: visibility is not a property of matter.
Trap 2: Empty bottles are empty.

When asked why water won't flow into a closed bottle, students often forget what is already inside it.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

The "empty" bottle is full of air, and air occupies space preventing the water from entering.

Always remember that invisible gases occupy space.
Trap 3: Water can be squeezed slightly.

In syringe experiments, students think pushing the plunger means the water compressed.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

Liquids have a definite volume. Only the air inside the syringe is being compressed.

Never state that water can be compressed.
Trap 4: Pumping air increases volume endlessly.

Because you can keep pumping air into a tire or castle, students say the volume of air keeps increasing.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

The container has a definite volume. Pumping more air means the air is compressed, which increases its mass but keeps volume the same.

Gases take the volume of their container.
Trap 5: Floating objects don't take up space.

When trying to measure volume via displacement, students think floating objects take up no space.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

Floating objects are not fully submerged, so they do not occupy space fully within the liquid, giving an inaccurate reading.

Volume measurement requires complete submersion.
Trap 6: The plastic ball expands in hot water.

Students state that the plastic shell of the ping pong ball expands to fix the dent.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

The air inside the ball gains heat and expands, pushing the plastic outward.

Always specify that the AIR expands, not the object.
Trap 7: Pouring changes liquid volume.

When water is moved to a taller container, the water looks like there is more of it.

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

Water has a definite volume but no definite shape, so only its shape changes.

State properties clearly to dispel visual illusions.
Trap 8: Holes stop water.

Students look at a cup without a hole and say "no hole means no water can enter."

Tap to reveal the truth
The Truth

The hole allows the trapped air to escape so the water can enter. Without a hole, air occupies space.

Explain the mechanism of air displacement.

EXPLAIN Phenomenon / Reason

Use this when asked why something happened (e.g. why water didn't enter).

[Observation] + BECAUSE + [Scientific Reason with keywords]

Real Example from a P4 Model Answer:

Air trapped inside Cup A takes up space and this prevents the water from entering Cup A.
What to AVOID:
Leaving out the observation and only stating the theory.
Using everyday words instead of "occupies space".

COMPARE Two Items

Use this when asked for a difference between properties or materials.

[Concept A property] + WHILE/WHEREAS/BUT + [Concept B property]

Real Example from a P4 Model Answer:

A solid has a definite shape but a liquid has no definite shape.
What to AVOID:
Only describing one side (e.g. "Solid has a definite shape."). You must explicitly state the other's property.

SUGGEST Action / Solution

Use this when asked for a way to achieve an outcome.

[Suggestion (action)] + BECAUSE + [Scientific reason]

Real Example from a P4 Model Answer:

Put the ping pong ball in water with a higher temperature.
What to AVOID:
Suggesting impossible or non-scientific actions.

STATE Fact / Relationship

Use this when asked to identify a property or state a direct relationship.

[Direct statement using accurate keywords]

Real Example from a P4 Model Answer:

Substance X has a definite volume and it does not have a definite shape.
What to AVOID:
Writing long explanations. "State" questions do not require "because".

GIVE_REASON For Observation

Use this when a specific outcome requires scientific justification.

[Scientific Fact/Keyword] + THEREFORE + [Outcome observed]

Real Example from a P4 Model Answer:

Air is matter and has mass, thus when more air is pumped in, the mass of air increases.
What to AVOID:
Stating the outcome without linking it back to the core property of matter.

Universal Open-Ended Answer Checklist

✓ Did you identify the specific substance (e.g. "air" instead of "the bottle")?
✓ Did you use scientific vocabulary (e.g. "occupies space", "compressed")?
✓ If comparing, did you describe BOTH items explicitly?
✓ Did you link the property directly to the outcome observed?
✓ Did you double check that you didn't say water is compressible?
